cases.hook: i changed the monthly mix. here’s why.
cases.label: CASE 01 / 04
cases.title: 4 LONG VIDEOS. 26 Shorts. ONE PLAN.
cases.brief: Grow an audience the brand owns, instead of renting reach with ads.
cases.myRole: Owned the content plan end to end: strategy, scripts, shoot schedule, SEO, reporting, and the budget across ads, creator Shorts and production.
cases.pullLine: Fewer, better pieces. A clear job for every format.
intro: Before the reset, the channel published six long-form videos a month and leaned on ads for reach. Subscribers kept climbing, but the audience data showed retention slipping.

I rebuilt the monthly plan around what the data rewarded: four long-form videos and twenty-six Shorts, with the podcast recorded on the long-form shoot day. Fewer, better pieces, and a clear job for every format.

sections.label: What the data said
body: Ad-driven views were inflating the totals. Once paid and organic were read separately, the pattern was clear: long-form earned the watch time, and Shorts brought in the subscribers. So I stopped treating every piece of content as equal and gave each format one job.

sections.label: How I sold it internally
body: Cutting output sounds like doing less. I made the case with the brand’s own data: which formats earned attention without ad support, and what each one was for. The plan was approved and became the monthly model.

cases.impactIntro: The channel over the same period.
cases.footnote: Source: YouTube Studio export. Subscriber growth is channel-wide. Organic views exclude paid ad campaigns.
cases.next: Give every format a business goal as well as a platform goal: long-form for search and consultations, Shorts for new audiences, the podcast for loyalty, each with its own number.

thumbs.alt: Mini chart of monthly output. Before: 6 long-form. After: 4 long-form, 26 Shorts, 1 podcast.

cases.hook: i built a podcast from a blank page.
cases.label: CASE 02 / 04
cases.title: I BUILT A podcast FROM A BLANK PAGE
cases.brief: Give a clinical brand a warmer, more human voice that people choose to spend time with.
cases.myRole: Proposed the format, wrote the scripts, co-hosted, and ran production and post-production.
cases.pullLine: Expert answers, without needing a medical degree.
intro: Clinikally Approved did not exist until I proposed it. A clinical brand needed a warmer voice, so I designed a format that puts a doctor’s expertise next to a curious everyday host asking the questions viewers actually have.
I co-host with Dr. Sarkar and Dr. Tasya, write the scripts, and produced the show from the first episode to the seventeenth.

evidence.title: Which Serum to Use? | Doctor’s Skincare Tips | Clinikally Approved Podcast
evidence.caption: which serum to use? the most-watched episode.

evidence.title: three script rules
lines: No jargon without a plain-language explanation.
Use Indian analogies: dahi, Delhi’s air quality, rupee prices.
Swap technical words for plain ones, like “good bacteria”.

sections.label: The format
body: Each episode follows a simple spine: a short intro from me, a numbered run of questions, and a clear outro. I play the curious, relatable voice. The doctor plays the expert. The audience gets answers without needing a medical degree.

sections.label: Beyond the show
body: I hosted and moderated the brand’s public webinar, “Uncomplicated: Skincare, Simplified by Dermatologists and AI”, with doctors, a nutritionist and a live demo of the brand’s AI routine builder.

impact.label: views on one episode, “Which Serum to Use?”

cases.next: Launch each episode clip-first, with three Shorts out before the full episode, and rotate guest doctors to widen reach without changing the format.

A large black softbox light in the foreground, with a camera on a tripod behind it.

cases.hook: one shoot day, six formats. here’s the system.
cases.label: CASE 03 / 04
cases.title: ONE SHOOT DAY. SIX formats.
cases.brief: A lean team cannot out-post bigger brands, so every shoot had to do several jobs.
cases.myRole: Designed the system and ran it: calendar, scripts, shoot batching, repurposing, SEO, approvals and publishing.
cases.result: 4 long-form + 26 Shorts + 1 podcast a month, from batched shoots.
cases.pullLine: A lean team can’t out-post bigger brands. It can out-plan them.
intro: I built a system where one shoot day with Dr. Sarkar feeds every format the channel runs. It rests on three habits: a standard script structure, batched shoots, and a repurposing pass that turns each recording into several pieces.
The result is a steady monthly cadence from a small team, with search built into every piece.

evidence.title: script order
evidence.caption: an illustration of structure, not data.

sections.label: The scripting standard: TSYS
body: Long-form videos were losing viewers at around the 50-second mark: the reason to care arrived too late. I built TSYS (Tell, Show, Yield, Summarize), a context-first structure that uses short teasers to front-load why the video matters. It became the channel’s long-form scripting standard.
list: Tell: say why it matters, up front.
Summarize: leave one thing to remember.

sections.label: One recording, many pieces, all searchable
body: Shoots are batched around the doctor’s time, and every podcast and long-form recording is cut for Shorts. I pull the moments from the transcript, so the clip list is ready before the edit starts. Every piece then ships with an SEO package: title options, a description, hashtags, search terms and tags, written around how people actually search.

sections.label: Beyond the channel
body: I scripted Instagram Shorts for creator partners, wrote vox pop question sets, and onboarded new doctors onto the shoot calendar, so the brand added voices without adding a new production process.

sections.label: The workflow
body: The editor cuts, the creative manager reviews, and I approve and publish. I owned the calendar, scripts, deadlines and final sign-off, and wrote the onboarding guide for new editors.

impact.label: long-form, Shorts and podcast episodes a month, from batched shoots.

cases.next: Turn the engine into templates and a shared clip library, so a second editor or a new channel can run it without me in the room.

thumbs.alt: A podcast studio with two people in orange armchairs, a large softbox light and a camera monitor.
Crew seated beside cameras, tripods, coiled cables and a monitor.

cases.label: CASE 04 / 04
cases.title: WHICH RESULTS WERE really OURS?
cases.brief: Show what content earned on its own, and connect it to the business.
cases.myRole: Built the reporting from YouTube Studio and store data, set the measurement rules the plan ran on, and presented performance and budget summaries to the founder.
cases.result: About 3x YouTube-referred store sessions, year on year.
cases.pullLine: Blended numbers flatter the team and mislead the plan.
intro: Total views can hide the story. Paid ad campaigns can account for most of a channel’s views, and they say very little about what the content earns by itself.
I built the reporting that separates paid from organic, then went a step further and traced content toward the store, so every plan started from what the content actually earned.

evidence.label: where the views came from
evidence.caption: share of channel views, about 13 months. source: YouTube Studio.

sections.label: How I split it
body: I export video-level data from YouTube Studio, tag the videos that were ad campaigns, and rebuild every total for organic content only. Then I read the trends by format: long-form, Shorts and podcast.

sections.label: From views to the store
body: Views are not the goal. I compared YouTube-referred store sessions year on year in Shopify, and they had grown about 3x. I also found that purchases completing in a separate checkout were invisible to the dashboard, so the reported conversion rate badly understated what content was driving. I recommended UTM links on every video so content could get credit for the sales it brings in.

impact.label: YouTube-referred store sessions, year on year.

cases.footnote: Sources: YouTube Studio export and Shopify. Paid and organic are reported separately.
cases.next: UTM links on every video from day one, and a monthly content-to-revenue report that sits next to the views report, not behind it.

about.statement: A JOURNALIST WHO LEARNED TO MAKE THE ALGORITHM CARE.
about.subLine: newsroom first. brands second. the audience always.
about.shortBio: I’m a content marketing manager in Gurugram, trained as a journalist at the Asian College of Journalism. I’ve written for Inc42, produced video for WION and CoinGape, run social for a real estate brand, and most recently owned a healthcare brand’s YouTube, podcast and creator content end to end. I plan around the audience, write for one person, and judge the work by what people actually did.

career.title: YouTube Manager
career.line: Owned the brand’s video content end to end: strategy, scripts, production, SEO, analytics and budget. Built the podcast, scripted creator Shorts and hosted the public webinar.

career.title: Video Producer
career.line: Produced founder-led video and branded editorial, and wrote features on startups and AI.

career.title: Video Journalist
career.line: Grew Instagram reach 38% with keyword-led content, and produced SEO-optimised explainer video for crypto and tech audiences.

career.title: Digital Journalist
career.line: Produced digital video for a 10.5M-subscriber channel, with videos reaching 1.6M+ views, and adapted broadcast news into digital-first formats.

career.title: Social Media Executive
career.line: Planned and ran community-led social campaigns, using engagement data to refine messaging.

about.lessonsHeading: Six things the job taught me
lessons: STRUCTURE IT BEFORE YOU STYLE IT.
NEVER ASSUME THE AUDIENCE IS STILL WATCHING.
KEEP PAID AND ORGANIC NUMBERS APART.
ASK WHAT THE NUMBER IS FOR.
